Witnesses are not required for purposes of acquiring it. Maggid Mishneh labors to explain why the possessor is believed against the creditor but not against the debtor. See there. One may explain that he understands Tosafot in Yevamot 115, s.v. Mai amrat, to hold that Rava is not concerned that the note fell or was deposited, but only that perhaps it was delivered to him. Thus it is certain that the creditor sold it to him, and the only doubt is whether there was a written assignment. If there was no writing, the seller can retract. The gloss in seif 1 states that even though he can retract, the purchaser may nevertheless retain the paper until his purchase money is returned. Since the note is therefore held by him like collateral, it appears that if both parties admitted to a sale by delivery without writing but disputed the purchase price, the purchaser would be believed to retain the paper up to the amount he claims. This resembles siman 72, Shach seif katan 94, regarding collateral known to have been given for a loan where the amount of the loan is unknown, in which case the creditor is believed. So too here. Since, had he claimed that the note was sold to him for the entire amount written in it, he would be believed to retain it to that amount, he is likewise believed through a migo when he claims that he purchased the note by writing and delivery and is entitled to the full value of the note. He may retain it until he receives that amount. This is also why he is believed if he claims that it was sold to him merely for use as paper, as Ran writes in Ketubot. As for Baal HaTerumot's challenge to Rambam from the end of Zeh Borer, where the Gemara says that the ruling follows Rabbi, who holds that documentary obligations are acquired by delivery, and the holder is believed through a migo that he purchased it, which implies that according to the view that documentary obligations are not acquired by delivery he could not claim purchase, see what I wrote above in siman 56.
And if there is proof that he sold it. See Shach, seif katan 31. His words are difficult to me. Since the purchaser has no migo, why should he be believed? We must say that there is a chazakah that one does not sell a paid note, as Tumim writes, except that when the purchaser has a migo he is believed because we find many instances in which a migo is accepted even against a chazakah, since not all chazakot are equal, as Tosafot write. Accordingly, if he does not wish to swear and says nothing as to when the note was paid, so that there is no migo, we certainly apply the above chazakah and assume that it was to be paid thereafter. The primary ruling is therefore Shach's first answer, that he must pay the full value of the note.
He takes a hesset oath. See Sema, seif katan 33, who writes that if Shimon claims, "I already paid, the note fell from me, and you found it," Shimon swears and is exempt both from Levi and from Reuven. Sema compares this to siman 41, where a note is found in the possession of another person and the creditor is believed with an oath, and Rama likewise rules in responsum 94, seif 2. At first glance this is difficult. Earlier in this seif it is stated that if Shimon claims that he paid Levi, Levi swears to Shimon and Reuven collects, which implies that even if Shimon says he paid Levi and the note then fell from Levi, Shimon is not believed. Moreover, in siman 72, in the case of Chanani and Chanan, it appears that even when the note is in Chanan's possession, Chanani collects, and it is not treated like a note found in another person's hand. It therefore appears as follows. Shach later, in siman 96, writes regarding a transfer in maamad sheloshtan that only the debt, not the document itself, is acquired. So long as the transferee has not received writing and delivery, because the document itself has not been acquired, the debtor is believed to claim payment. Once writing and delivery are subsequently given, it again becomes a debt evidenced by a note. Shach similarly writes in seif katan 65 that until the document itself has been acquired, the debt has the status of an oral loan, until writing and delivery are given. Accordingly, a distinction should be made. When Levi litigates with Shimon, since according to Rambam Reuven is believed regarding his acquisition and has acquired the note, Levi is left as one asserting an oral claim because the note is not in his possession, and Shimon is therefore believed against him. But when Levi later gives writing and delivery to Reuven, the debt again becomes a loan evidenced by a note in Reuven's possession, and Shimon can no longer claim payment against him. In any event the note belongs to Reuven: if Levi already gave him writing and delivery it is his, and if he did not do so earlier, he gives it to him now. According to Rama's gloss, who holds that Reuven is not believed regarding acquisition, the note is legally regarded as though it were still in Levi's hand, since Reuven is obligated to return it to him. It is therefore a debt evidenced by a note in Levi's possession. This also explains siman 42: whenever the law requires the document to be returned to the creditor, the claim is a full debt evidenced by a note; only where the document is not legally to be returned to him is it treated as an oral debt. See also what I wrote in siman 65, Biurim seif katan 6. Tumim likewise agrees that the debtor is not believed to claim payment, although he gives no reason, and he contradicts what he himself wrote at the end of siman 41, that even where beit din returned the note into the custodian's hand, the debtor is believed because the creditor has no migo, all the more so here. I have already rejected his position there as well.
Also with respect to acquiring it. The reason is stated by Ran in Perek HaKotev regarding a bundle of notes. Ramban, in Sefer HaZechut, writes that specifically with movable property, or with documents according to the view that documentary obligations are acquired by delivery, since possession itself effects acquisition, the possessor is also considered a muchzak by virtue of that possession. A promissory note that requires both writing and delivery is different. Since delivery alone is not an act of acquisition, possession of the paper does not make him a muchzak. For the same reason he is not believed to say that he acquired it through agav or by a gift of a shechiv mera, because his physical possession does not give him the legal status of a muchzak.
It is held by the third party, even though he is believed against the seller. At first glance this is difficult. A third party should not be more credible than the litigant himself. If the note were in the purchaser's own hand he would not be believed regarding acquisition, so on what basis is the third party believed? Tumim likewise raises this difficulty. Upon examination, however, there is no difficulty. Sema in siman 64, seif katan 20, explains why there the holder is believed through a migo that he could deny the transaction entirely and may therefore retain the note, whereas here he is not believed even merely to retain it. There he claims only that the note is collateral and has a migo. Here he claims that he bought it and seeks to collect through it. His alternative claim of complete denial would not enable him to collect, and therefore it is not a valid migo even for retaining the note. It is a migo for only half of the asserted claim. This, I believe, is Sema's intent. A third party is different. The law is that a third party is believed even if he has no present migo, provided that at some earlier time he had the ability to act accordingly, as explained in siman 56. Tosafot in Gittin 64 explain that whenever the depositor placed him in a position where at some time he could have brought about a particular result, the depositor empowered him so that the legal result follows the third party's statement even if that statement is false. Thus, regarding acquisition in the limited sense that the purchaser may retain the paper, the third party at some point had the ability to accomplish that result. He could have delivered the note to the purchaser, and the purchaser could then have claimed that he acquired the paper merely for its material value, a claim on which he would be believed, as Ran writes in Ketubot. Such a claim would allow him to retain the note until all the money he claims is paid, even up to the entire amount of the note, as explained above. Alternatively, the third party could have enabled him to say that the note was pledged to him for the full amount. The depositor therefore trusted the third party to establish that result by his statement, even falsely, because whatever result the third party could once have produced was entrusted to his word. But as to collecting the debt, the third party could never have effected that result merely by his own act, and therefore his statement does not suffice. Although his statement is ineffective for collection, it is effective for possession, because we divide the statement. There are two distinct acquisitions in the sale of a note. Acquisition of the paper for its physical use is a Torah acquisition, while acquisition of the right to collect is rabbinic. Although the third party is not believed to permit collection, he is believed as to the paper itself, because the depositor entrusted him as to that which he could have effected even if he were to speak falsely. By contrast, when the note is in the purchaser's own possession, the purchaser can be believed only through a present migo. Since he seeks to collect through his asserted purchase, the alternative claim would support only part of his position, and there is no migo for half a claim. He is therefore not believed at all. This appears clear.
And the purchaser cannot collect. See Shach, seif katan 42, who asks why this is not a case of one who is obligated to take an oath but cannot swear, and therefore must pay, in light of the third party's testimony. At first glance this is very difficult, as Tumim also notes. First, the claim involves a lien on land, for which there is no Torah oath. Second, the debtor can say, "What concern is this oath to me? I will deposit the money with beit din, and they can do with it whatever the law requires." If Reuven had a deposit in Shimon's possession and Levi came with one witness saying that Reuven sold him the deposit, would Shimon be required to hand it over because he is unable to take an oath? That would amount to extracting money on the testimony of one witness, which is certainly not the law. There is no oath imposed on the debtor or custodian in such a case. Upon examination, however, the second objection is not difficult. In the custodial case described by Tumim, there is no oath because the custodian has no personal benefit in denying Levi. He wishes to return the property but does not know to whom, so he deposits it with beit din and withdraws from the dispute. Here, by contrast, the document is held by a third party whom Rama rules is believed against the seller. Consequently, if the debtor does not plead against the purchaser, "You are not my litigant," the money is paid to the purchaser, because the third party is believed regarding the purchaser's acquisition. This follows the Mechaber's presentation of Rambam's view that the possessor is believed as to acquisition, so that if the debtor does not raise that defense, payment goes to the purchaser. Therefore, even if the debtor deposits the money with beit din here, beit din will deliver it to the purchaser. The debtor is exempt only when he affirmatively pleads to the purchaser, "You are not my litigant." That denial serves solely the debtor's own interest by preventing the purchaser from receiving the money, since without it the money would be delivered to the purchaser. It is therefore properly treated as a case of one who is obligated to swear but cannot swear. This is straightforward. This analysis, however, follows Shach's view that the third party is fully believed. According to what I wrote above, seif katan 19, that the third party is believed only to permit retention of the note while the debtor may still pay the original creditor, the rule of one who cannot swear does not apply. The first objection, that this is a lien on land, is also not difficult, because Shach's question applies at least to a note without property liability or to a handwritten obligation. Since the Mechaber speaks without qualification, his ruling includes such cases. As for Ketzot HaChoshen's statement that documents are excluded from the law of oaths, I do not understand it. The claim here concerns the money represented by the document, not the document itself. Moreover, even a note containing property liability may be regarded here as having lost its effective lien, because according to Sema, seif katan 33, the debtor can discharge himself, and here likewise the holder is believed regarding acquisition but not regarding the underlying claim while the note is in a third party's possession. Purchasers of the debtor's land can also say to the note purchaser, "You are not our litigant," and the rule of one who is obligated to swear but cannot do so does not apply to purchasers. Just as we expound that the oath of Hashem is "between the two of them," excluding heirs, so too it excludes purchasers. Since the note's force against encumbered property has thereby been impaired, denial is not considered denial of a land lien, as explained at the end of siman 62 where the debtor claims that half has been paid and witnesses testify that all was paid. Nor can one challenge the present ruling from Shach in siman 98, seif katan 12, who writes that when in any event the money will leave the defendant's possession, a definite claim prevails over an uncertain one. Here too, it might be argued, the money will go either to the creditor or to the purchaser, so the purchaser's definite claim that he bought the note should prevail over the debtor's uncertainty. This is no difficulty. There, at least, the defendant is a litigant vis a vis the shopkeeper because he instructed the shopkeeper to incur the expense. Here the purchaser is not the debtor's litigant at all, and the debtor need not answer his claim. The purchaser therefore cannot prevail by a forced either way argument. This is simple.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he:
על גבי קרקע. ולפמש"ל דלא בעי כתיבה באגב נאמן אף לענין תביעה:
ואם יש ראיה שמכר. וה"ה אם אין לו ראיה רק שלוה מוד' שמכרו חייב לשלם כל דמי השטר ש"ך בתירוץ הראשון וכ"מ וע"ב ואם יש נאמנות בשטר או שהוא תוך זמנו אין צריך שבוע':
וכן אם הודה. ובמקום שא"י למחול כמבואר לקמן לא מהני הודאת המוכר:
ישלם לוי. ואם אומר שנפרע מקודם אם יש ראיה שמכר חייב לשלם כל דמי השטר ואם אין ראיה רק שמודה נאמן במיגו דאי בעי היה אומר שלא מכר לו ואין חילוק בין אומר שנפרע או שאומר שטעה בחשבון ש"ך:
משלמין. העיקר כהסמ"ע דאין חייבים לשלם רק מנכסים שירשו ולא מנכסי עצמן ודלא כש"ך:
טען לוי. פשוטן של דברים שלוי טוען אמת נפרעתי אבל לא מכרתי לך נשבע היסת נגדו ואולם הסמ"ע בשם הב"י כתב עוד דאם טוען הלו' פרעתי וממני נפל דנשבע ונפטר מלוי ומראובן הואיל ואין השטר ביד המלו' וע"ב) (דדוקא המלוה אינו גוב' כיון שהלוקח נאמן לענין קנייתו והוי כאין לו שטר אבל כשיתן לו כתיבה להלוקח הלוקח גובה בשטר ואין הלוה נאמן בטענ' נפיל' וכן לדעת הרב דאף לענין קנייתו א"נ וצריך להחזיר השטר והמוכר גובה בו ואין הלוה נאמן נגדו:
שגם לענין קנייתו. הטעם ע"ב והלכך אם פרע הלוה להלוקח בלא ידיעת המוכר חוזר וגובה ממנו ואם הלו' טוען ברי לי שהי' בידי שטר כתיב' ואבד נשבע היסת ונפטר כיון שכבר הוציא השטר וקרעו ש"ך ולענין אם נאמן להחזיק גוף הנייר יש בו מחלוקת התוספת פרק הכותב והר"ן שם:
וכנ"ל. וה"ה אם טוען שנתנו לו במתנת שכ"מ ואם הם שטרות שניקנין במסירה לבד נאמן אפילו נגד הלו' ואם יש עדים שנפל הימנו לכ"ע אף בשטרות שניקנין במסירה לבד צריך להביא ראי' דאין ראיה במה שהשטר בידו דשמא מצאו כיון שידוע שנפל משא"כ בעלמא לא חיישינן לנפיל' ובשני יב"ש ואחד יש לו שטר על לוה ומודה שאינו שלו וטוען שנמכר לו מיב"ש השני לגבי מוכר נאמן במיגו שהי' אומר שהיא שלו מתחלה ולגבי לוה יש בו מחלוקת הפוסקים אי נאמן במיגו כיון דהוי מיגו להוציא רק דהוי במקום שטר וע' בכ"מ תומים:
תח"י שליש. ומיירי שהשליש הוא קרוב או אשה אבל אם הוא עד כשר מחוייב הלו' לשלם להלוקח כיון שהוא א"י אם מכר לזה והשליש הוי ע"א הוי הלו' משואיל"מ אכן למאי דקיימא לן דלא שייך משואי"ל בלא הו"ל למידע אפילו השליש כשר א"נ נגד תביעתו ש"ך וע"ב:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en:
By means of land. According to what was written above that transfer by agav requires no separate writing, the purchaser is believed even for purposes of suing on the debt:
And if there is proof that he sold. The same applies if there is no independent proof but the borrower himself admits that the document was sold. He must then pay the full value of the document, Shach in his first answer, and this appears correct. See Beurim. If the document contains a credibility clause or the debt is still within its fixed term, no oath is required:
And likewise if he admitted. In a circumstance where the seller no longer has power to waive the debt, as explained below, his later admission is likewise ineffective:
He shall pay Levi. If the seller says that the debt had already been paid before the sale, then if there is proof of the sale he must pay the full value of the document. If there is no proof and he merely admits the sale, he is believed through a migo that he could have denied selling it. There is no distinction whether he says the borrower paid him or says that the debt amount was based on a mistaken calculation, Shach:
They pay. The primary ruling follows the Sema that the heirs are liable only from property they inherited, not from their own assets, unlike the Shach:
Levi claimed. The straightforward reading is that Levi says, "It is true that I was paid, but I never sold the document to you." He swears a hesset oath against the purchaser. The Sema, in the name of the Beit Yosef, adds that if the borrower says, "I paid and the document later fell from me," he swears and is exempt toward both Levi and Reuven because the document is no longer in the lender's possession. See Beurim. This applies only to the original lender, who cannot collect because the purchaser is believed regarding his acquisition and the lender is therefore treated as though he has no document. If the seller provides the purchaser with the required written assignment, the purchaser may collect on the document and the borrower is not believed merely to claim that it fell from him. Likewise, according to the Rama, who holds that the possessor is not believed even regarding the acquisition and therefore must return the document, the seller may then collect with it and the borrower is not believed against him:
Also with respect to his acquisition. See Beurim for the reason. Therefore, if the borrower paid the purchaser without the seller's knowledge, the seller may collect from the borrower again. If the borrower makes a definite claim that a written assignment had been in his possession and was lost, he swears hesset and is exempt because he had already produced and destroyed the original debt document, Shach. There is a dispute in Tosafos and the Ran in Kesubos whether the purchaser is believed to retain the physical paper itself:
As above. The same applies if he claims that the debt document was given to him as a deathbed gift. If it is a type of document acquired by delivery alone, he is believed even against the borrower. If there are witnesses that the document fell from its owner, then according to all opinions even a document normally acquired by delivery alone requires proof of a valid transfer, because possession proves nothing when it is known that the document was lost and may have been found. Ordinarily we do not suspect loss. Where two people have identical names and one holds a document against a borrower but admits that the document was not originally his, claiming that it was sold to him by the other person with the same name, he is believed against the alleged seller through a migo that he could have claimed original ownership. Against the borrower, the decisors dispute whether such a migo is sufficient because it is a migo used to extract money, though it is supported by a document. See Kesef Mishnah and Tumim:
In the possession of a third party. The case assumes that the third party is a relative or a woman. If he is a qualified witness, the borrower may be obligated to pay the purchaser because the borrower does not know whether the document was sold, while the third party constitutes one witness, creating the rule of one who cannot swear and therefore must pay. However, according to our ruling that this principle does not apply where the defendant had no reason to know the fact, even a qualified third party is not believed against the borrower's claim, Shach. See Beurim:

pitchei_teshuva.he: אין יכולין לגבותו. עבה"ט שכתב והש"ך כתב דדין זה צ"ע כו' וע' בת' נאות דשא סי' ס"ח שכתב דע"כ מיירי שראו השטר בידו מתחל' קודם שמכרו להעדים (וסתמא דמלתא מיירי בהכי דהא מכירת השטר בכומ"ס מן הסתם הוא בפני עדים א"כ הרי ראו העדים ביד המלו' את השטר קודם שמכרו להעדים בכתיב' ומסיר') דהמחבר פוסל אפילו בכה"ג משום דחיישי' שמעיקרא חתמו בשקר אדעתא דהכי כדי שיקנו השטר אח"כ ואהא פליג הש"ך דשנים אין חשודים בכך אבל היכא דלא ראו השטר בידו מעיקרא ודאי השטר בטל דכיון דעכשיו הם נוגעים חיישי' דהשתא כתבוהו והקדימו זמנו בכוונ' וזה נ"ל ברור ע"ש ועמ"ש לעיל סי' מ"ו סל"ה ס"ק י"ב:
pitchei_teshuva.en: They cannot collect it. See Baer Heitev, who cites the Shach that this ruling requires study. See Responsa Naot Deshe, siman 68, who writes that the case must be one where the witnesses saw the note in the lender’s possession before he sold it to them. Ordinarily this is indeed the case, because a sale of a debt instrument by writing and delivery is generally performed before witnesses, so those witnesses saw the note in the lender’s possession before he transferred it to them. The Mechaber nevertheless disqualifies the note even in such a case because we suspect that from the outset they signed falsely with the intention of later acquiring the note. The Shach disagrees on the ground that two witnesses are not suspected of such conduct. But where they did not see the note in his possession beforehand, the note is certainly invalid. Since the witnesses are now financially interested, we suspect that they wrote it only now and intentionally antedated it. This appears clear. See there, and see what I wrote above, siman 46, seif 35, seif katan 12.

rabbi_akiva_eiger.he: [שו"ע] ואם מת הלוה קודם. נ"ב הי' הלוה במדינ' אחרת וקנה השטר קודם ששמע בו שמת אע"פ שאח"כ שמעו בו שמת דינו כמת לוה אחר שקנאו ריק"ש בשם ת' הר"ן סי' ל"א:
rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: [Shulchan Aruch] And if the borrower died before. Note: If the borrower was in another country and the purchaser acquired the deed before hearing that he had died, even though they afterward learned that the borrower had already died, the law is the same as where the borrower died after the purchaser acquired it. Maharikash in the name of Responsa Ran, siman 31.

siftei_kohen.he:
[" אינו צריך עדים לענין קנייתו. והרבה חולקים בזה והכי קי\"ל דצריך עדים גם לענין קנייתו וכדלקמן והלכך אם פרע הלוה ללוקח בלא ידיעת המוכר חוזר וגובה ממנו וכמו שיתבאר לקמן סעי' י\"ז וכ\"כ הב\"ח מיהו אם הלוה טוען ברור לי שהיה לו שטר כתיבה ואבד נשבע היסת ונפטר:"]
[" או שטען שהקנוהו לו אג\"ק. היינו לשטת הרמב\"ם והמחבר דלעיל סעיף י' דבאג\"ק לא בעי כתיבה אבל לפי מ\"ש שם בס\"ק כ\"ו דבאג\" אינו אלא במקום מסירה וכתיבה בעי לא שייך הכא לומר כן וק\"ל (עיין בתשובת מהרי\"ט סי' צ\"א):"]
[" ואם יש ראיה שמכר כ\"כ ה' המגיד והקשה בס' גי' תרומה שער נ\"א סוף ח\"ד דף שי\"ב אמאי כתב המגיד דישראי' אפי' ליכא ראי' והוא מודה נמי וענין מגו לא שייך הכא דלא אמרי' מגו אלא להאמין בטענה א' מגו דאי בעי טעין אחרת והוי כמגו לאפטורי משבועה עכ\"ל ול\"ק מידי דפשיטא דהודאת בע\"ד כק' עדים דמי ועוד נראה דדוקא קא' אם יש ראיה משום דר\"ל דחייב לשלם לראובן כל דמי השטר ואי ליכא ראיה שמכר אע\"פ שמודה שמכר ואינו רוצה לישבע מ\"מ במה שאינו רוצה לישבע אין הכרח שנפרע אחר המכירה דלמא נפרע קודם לכן ונהי דכשמודה המוכר בפירוש שנפרע אח\"כ חייב לשלם כל דמי השטר מ\"מ אי הוה אמר שנפרע קודם לכן ואינו חייב לשלם רק המעות שקבל נאמן במגו דאי בעי אמר לא מכרתי והלכך השתא נמי נהי דאינו רוצה לישבע דלמא אינו רוצה לישבע מחמת שנפרע קודם לכן אבל אם יש ראיה שמכר דלית ליה מגו אין מאמינים אותו לו' שנפרע קודם לכן וכמ\"ש לקמן ס\"ק ל\"ה בשם ה' המגיד והלכך כיון דאינו רוצה לישבע אין אנו מאמיני' אותו שנפרע קודם לכן וכיון דהשתא בגרמתו מזיקו חייב לשלם לו כל דמי השטר כן נ\"ל:"]
[" חייב לשלם לראובן. אע\"פ שלא הודה שפרעו (דוקא כשאמר שמעון ישבע לי וכמ\"ש בס\"ק שאח\"ז ע\"ש) ומחויב לשלם כל דמי השטר ולא סגי כשמחזיר לו הדמים שקבל כל זה משמע מה' המגיד שם וכ\"כ בסמ\"ע ס\"ק ל\"א להדיא ואע\"ג דבה' המגיד שם לא כתוב שצריך לשלם לו כל דמי השטר רק בהודה שפרעו מ\"מ משמע שם בהרב המגיד להדיא דה\"ה הכא כיון שאינו רוצה לישבע הרי הוא כמודה שפרעו כיון שבגרמתו נפסד השטר וכן הוא בשלטי גבורים בשם ריא\"ז שהבאתי לק' סעיף ל\"ב ס\"ק ק\"ט ועיקר:"]
[" וכן אם הודה כו'. לשון וכן שכ' המחבר מגומגם הוא וה\"ל למימר וכ\"ש אם הודה לוי שפרעו: מיהו הא דאם אינו רוצה לישבע חייב לשלם לראובן היינו דוקא כשאומר שמעון ישבע לי וכמ\"ש הרמב\"ם והמחבר אבל אם אינו אומר ישבע לי אע\"פ שאומר שפרע לו כיון דאינו מחוייב לישבע וכדלקמן סי' פ\"ב סעיף ב' גובה ראובן וכן מ\"ש אח\"כ יורשיו נשבעין כו' היינו דוקא כשאומר להם הלוה אשתבעו לי וכמ\"ש לק' סי' ק\"ח סעיף ה' ע\"ש:"]
[" אם הודה לוי שפרעו כו'. בבעה\"ת שער נ\"א ח\"א כתב ע\"ז וז\"ל ומסתברא דוקא דלא כתוב ביה נאמנות אבל אם יש בו נאמנות מוציא ממנו בעל כרחו ואין הודאת המלוה מועלת כלום לסברתם שפסקו שנאמן לומר שטר היה לי ואבד דחיישינן לקנוני' עכ\"ל ולא נהירא לי דכיון שהמלוה אומר שפרוע מה בכך שיש בו נאמנות מ\"מ הרי הוא עצמו או' שהוא פרוע וכמ\"ש לעיל סי' ע\"ז ס\"ק ד' ועוד דהא טעמא הוא משום דנאמן לומר פרוע במגו דאי בעי מחיל או משום שהרי הוא כמוחלו עתה וכמו שיתבאר בס\"ק שאח\"ז וא\"כ זה שייך אף בנאמנות וכן משמע מדברי הרמב\"ם והט\"ו ושאר פוסקים שלא חילקו בכך וכן עיקר ונ\"מ אף להחולקים שאין נאמן לומר שטר היה לי ואבד היכא שיש בידו כתיבה:"]
[" הודה לוי שפרעו כו'. דין זה אפי' ביש עדים לראובן מהקנייה שהרי היה לוי יכול למחול את החוב ומגו דאי בעי מצי מחיל כי אמר שטרא פרוע הוא נאמן ויש מי שכתב דכי אמר שטרא פרוע הרי הוא כמוחלו עכשיו ואין לך מחילה גדולה מזו עכ\"ל ה' המגיד שם וכן הבאתי לק' סעיף ט\"ז ס\"ק ס\"א בשם הצרפתים ובשם הר\"מ בן יוד' דפרוע היא מחילה ומ\"ש הרא\"ש והר\"ן ס\"פ כל הנשבעין שהמוכר נאמן לומר פרוע במיגו דאי בעי מחיל ליה לרווחא דמלתא כתבו כן ולפ\"ז לאו דוקא פרוע אלא כל דבר שמבטל השטר כגון אמנה ותנאי וכה\"ג נאמן המוכר וכ\"כ ר' ירוחם סוף נתיב י\"ד ומביאו ב\"י סימן זה סי\"ד וגם בס\"ס זה דנאמן המוכר לומר אמנה הוא או פרוע רק שכתב דנאמן במגו דאי בעי מחיל ליה ולפי מ\"ש אין צריך למגו אלא כך לי אמנה ותנאי ופרוע כמחילה מיהו מדברי הרא\"ש פ\"ב דכתובות גבי כשחייב לאחרים ואומר פרוע הוא דאינו נאמן במגו דאי בעי מחיל ליה משום דאין בדעתו למחול ולהפסיד חובו וכ\"כ ר' ירוחם נ\"ו ח\"ו לא משמע כן דאם כן אמאי לא יהא נאמן לומר פרוע דהא לדבריהם יכול למחול אף היכא שחייב לאחרים ופרעון גופיה מחילה היא מ\"מ נ\"ל עיקר כמ\"ש דסבר' גדולה היא דמה לי מוחלו ומה לי אומר שפרוע הוא ס\"ס לפי דבריו נמחל השטר ונתבטל במה שאומר שהוא פרוע ואין לך מחילה גדולה מזה וכן העליתי לקמן סי' פ\"ו סעיף ה' ס\"ק י\"א ע\"ש ולפ\"ז אין צריך לפרש הא דאמרינן בש\"ס סוף פרק שנים אוחזין ריש (בבא מציעא דף כ') ש\"מ איתא לדשמואל כמו שפירשו יש פוסקים משום דאי לקנוני' הוי בעיא היה לה למחול אלא פירש כפשוטו דהשתא דנותנת לו שובר ואומרת שכתובת' פרוע אין לך מחילה גדולה מזה ואיתא לדשמואל דאמר המוכר שט\"ח לחבירו וחזר ומחלו מחול (ושמואל רבותא קאמר דאפי' מחלו לו בחנם מחול וכ\"ש כשאומר פרוע או אמנה שהוא בטל) וכ\"כ הנ\"י שם בס\"פ דמציעא דלאו עדין מגו אתינא עלה אלא דכיון דקא מודה דפרוע היא ושובר מעליא הוא זו היא מחילת' וכמאן דאמרה מחול לך דמי עכ\"ל ומשמע שם בנ\"י שדבריו הם לקוחים מדברי הרשב\"א והר\"ן ע\"ש וכן נראה מפירש\"י שם וז\"ל ש\"מ מדלא חיישי' להכי דאי נמי הוה הכי שפיר זכה בעל בשובר שנכתב לשמה איתא לדשמואל כו' הלכך אם מכרה זו כתובתה באייר וחזרתה ומחלתה לבעל בתשרי מחול ושפיר טריף בעל עכ\"ל ולאו דוקא כתבה שובר אלא ה\"ה אומרת שהוא פרוע אלא שהשובר הוא לראיה שהכתוב' פרוע ואע\"פ שהבעה\"ת שער נ\"א ריש חלק ב' הביא ל' תשובת הראב\"ד במוכר שט\"ח לחבירו שאינו נאמן לומר פרוע במיגו דאי בעי מחיל ושמעתתא דבבא מציעא מוכח כן דקתני מצא שובר בשוק וכו' ואם איתא דבדבורא בעלמא יכולה להפסיד הלקוחות מאי טעמא איירי בשובר כו' עכ\"ל אין נ\"ל כן אלא כמ\"ש וגם בלא\"ה הא הרמב\"ן והרא\"ש והר\"ן ס\"פ כל הנשבעין ושאר פוסקים והרמב\"ם וה' המגיד והמחבר כאן וכן הבעל העיטור ובעה\"ת והטור והמחבר לקמן סעיף ט\"ו ודאי דלא ס\"ל הכי דהא כתבו להדיא המוכר שט\"ח נאמן המוכר לומר פרוע אלא ודאי צ\"ל כדפי' דהא דנקט בש\"ס שובר משום שהשובר הוא לראיה אי נמי משום סיפא דהיכא דאין האשה מודה לא יחזיר לא לזה ולא לזה אבל אה\"נ שנאמנת בדיבורה לבד שהכתובה היא פרוע במגו דאי בעיא מחלה ליה או מטעם שכתבתי דכיון שהיא אימרת שהיא פרוע אין לך מחיל' גדול' מזו ודלא כתשובת הראב\"ר וכן עיקר:"]
[" ישלם לוי לראובן כו'. טען לוי שלא מכר ולא נתן כו' ז\"ל ה' המגיד ממה שאמר רבינו ז\"ל ולא נתן יראה לי שדעתו ז\"ל כשאמר לוי שפרוע הוא משלם לראובן כדין מוחל שנתבאר (לקמן סעיף ל\"ב) שחייב לשלם כל מה שבשטר ר\"ל שאפי' מכרו במנה ושוה אלף מוציאין מן המוחל אלף אף כאן כשאומר פרוע הוא משלם כל שווי השטר ואין אנו מאמינים אותו לומר פרוע היה קודם המכירה (נ\"ל דהיינו דוקא שיש עדים שמכרו לו דאל\"כ נאמן לימר שנפרע קודם לכן במגו דלא מכרתי ואע\"ג דאם. היה אומר לא מכרתי היה מעיז והשתא אינו מעיז שפיר אמרי' מגו בכה\"ג כמ\"ש לקמן סי' פ\"א סעיף כ\"ג ס\"ק נ\"ח וסי' צ\"ג סעיף ב' וכן הוכחתי לקמן ס\"ס פ\"ב בדיני מגו אות ו') ולא ישלם אלא דמים שקיבל דנמצא מקח שאינו מקח ואע\"פ שאנו מאמינים אותו לענין הלוה היינו משים דמצי מחיל אבל ודאי הוא חייב בתשלומין כמו שהי' מתחייב אם מחל ואם לא תאמר כן אפי' הודה לוי שנתן לא ישלם כלום אם אנו מאמינים אותו שכבר נפרע קודם נתינה דה\"ל כנותן מה שאינו ויש לדחות ולו' שכוונ' רבינו הוא באמרו ולא נתן לא נתן כך באחריו' אי נמי לא נתן ואח\"כ נפרע מ\"מ עיקר הדין נ\"ל כמ\"ש עכ\"ל ודבריו נכונים גם דעת הרמב\"ם נראה כן ומ\"ש ויש לדחות כו' הוא דוחק וכן הבאתי לקמן סעיף ל\"ב ס\"ק ק\"ט השלטי גבורים בשם ריא\"ז וכ\"נ דעת המחבר ועיקר (ומשמע דאע\"פ שלא פרע לו כל דמי השטר אלא שטוען שפרע לו כפי סך שקבל בעד המכירה ובזה נתרצה שיהא השטר פרוע צריך לשלם לו כל דמי השטר כיון שבגרמתו נפסד השטר) ואין להקשות ממ\"ש הבעה\"ת והט\"ו לקמן סעיף ל\"ד דאם הוציא הלוה שובר ששטר זה פרוע ה\"ז מקח טעות והמעות חוזרים משמע שא\"צ להחזיר אלא המעות שקבל דשאני התם שמוציא שובר א\"כ אפי' בלא הודאת המוכר מתברר שמכר לו שטר פרוע והוי מקח טעות והדמים חוזרים משא\"כ הכא שאינו מתברר שהוא פרוע אם לא ע\"פ הודאת לוי שהרי אם היה רוצה לוי לישבע היה ראובן גובה בע\"כ של שמעון א\"כ מכח הודאת לוי או מכח שאינו רוצה לישבע דהוי כהודא' אינו גובה ראובן והוי כמוחלו עתה ומזיקו שבגרמת לוי עתה הוא נפסד השטר הלכך צריך לשלם לו כל דמי השטר וכן נראה שמחלק בשלטי גבירים בשם ריא\"ז שהבאתי לקמן סעיף ל\"ב ס\"ק ק\"ט ועיקר. ובזה נלפע\"ד דלא קשה מה שהקשה הרא\"ש ס\"פ שנים אוחזין אהא דאמרינן התם ש\"מ איתא לדשמואל כו' דהא אי תמחול תצטרך לשלם לו כל דמי הכתובה וכתב שיש רוצים לומר מכח קושיא זו דבמחול א\"צ לשלם רק דמים שקבל מן הלוקח ולפענ\"ד דצריך לשלם כל דמי השטר וכמ\"ש לקמן סעיף ל\"ב ס\"ק ק\"ט ושפיר קאמר התם בש\"ס ש\"מ איתא לדשמואל משום דהשתא נמי צריכים לשלם ללוקח כל דמי השטר דהא אין מחזירים השובר אלא ע\"פ הודאת' ואי לאו שהיתה מודה לא היו מחזירין לו השובר נמצא שבגרמתה נפסד הכתוב' והרי היא כמוחלת עתה הכתוב' כנ\"ל ברור (וכן נראה להדיא מדברי הנ\"י פ\"ק דמציע' ע\"ש):"]
[" ואם לא רצו לישבע משלמין ללוקח. משמע שמשלמין לו כל מה שהי' שוה השטר וכן משמע בה' המגיד ועוד לפי מה שפי' בסמ\"ע ס\"ק ל\"א דעת המחבר מ\"ש חייב לשלם ראובן היינו כל דמי השטר א\"כ מסתמא גם מ\"ש המחבר כאן משלמין ללוקח פירושו כל דמי השטר דמסתמ' כל מה שאביהן הי' חייב חייבין הם ג\"כ ועוד דמסתמא מיירי בחד גוונ' דאל\"כ ה\"ל לפרש ולא לסתום ועוד דאין טעם לחלק בין אביהם להם עצמם דאין סברא לומר כיון שאביהן הי' המוכר יתחייב יותר דהא חייב לשלם יותר ממה שקבל דמי המכיר' וגם אפי' נתן במתנה חייב לשלם אלא ודאי החיוב הוא כיון שאינו רוצה לישבע וגורם ללוקח היזק בזה חייב מדינא דגרמי לשלם לו הזיקו א\"כ האי טעמא שייך נמי ביורשים מה תאמר שהיורשים אמרו אנו אין מתכוונים להזיק אלא שאנו יודעים שהוא פרוע ואין אנו רוצם לישבע שקר א\"כ גם המוכר או הנותן יאמר טענה זו אלא ודאי כיון שאינו מברר טענתו חייב מדינא דגרמי וכמ\"ש לקמן סעיף ל\"ב ס\"ק ק\"ה בשם שלטי גבורים בשם ריא\"ז וא\"כ ה\"ה גבי יורשים וזה ברור ומכאן גם כן סתיר' על דברי הסמ\"ע דלקמן סעיף ט\"ו ס\"ק מ\"א וכמ\"ש שם בס\"ק נ\"ג ע\"ש:"]
[" טען לוי שלא מכר כו' כלומר לוי טוען כן נגד ראובן נשבע לוי כו' אבל בב\"י וכ\"מ פירשו שלוי טוען כן נגד שמעון נשבע שמעון ולא מחוור ובסמ\"ע ס\"ק ל\"ג כתב דהא דלא פירשו כפשוטו משום דס\"ל דאם מודה לטי שנפרע וטוען נגד ראובן לא מכרתיו לך אפי' שבועה א\"צ לעשות לוי נגדו דהמע\"ה עכ\"ל ולא נהירא דלמה לא ישבע לוי הלא לפי דברי ראובן חייב לשלם לו בברי וכך הם פשט דברי הרמב\"ם וכן פי' ה' המגיד להדיא ומביאו ב\"י וגם הר\"ב רמ\"א כתב בתשו' סי' צ\"ה שאלה ב' דנשבע לוי ושגם הב\"י סובר כן רק שהב\"י מוסיף מדעתו שגם שמעון נשבע היסת וכ\"כ הב\"ח דגם הב\"י מודה לזה לדינא וכ\"כ העיר שושן דלוי נשבע ע\"ש:"]
[" שגם לענין קנייתו כו'. עיין בעיר שושן שכתב שצריך להחזיר לו גוף הנייר וכן הוא בבעה\"ת שער נ\"א ר\"ח בשם ה\"ר נתן ב\"ר מאיר וכ\"כ הר\"ן פ' הכותב גבי עובדא דמלוגי דשטרי כמ\"ש לעיל סי' ס\"ד ס\"ק ד' ע\"ש:"]
[" אינו נאמן ומשמע דה\"ה אם טוען נתנו לי במתנת ש\"מ אינו נאמן ודלא כמ\"ש ב\"י בא\"ע סי' פ\"ו וז\"ל בתשוב' להרמב\"ן סי' ל' ולענין ש\"ח שטענו האפוטרופסים אם טענה שהבעל נתנה לה הדין עם האפטרופס שהשטר אינו נקנה אלא בכתיב' ומסירה ואפי' ליכא עדים וראה דהא לא שייך בשטרות מגו וכמ\"ש הרי\"ף פ' הכותב במלוג' דשטרי ע\"כ ומיהו אם אומרת שנתנו לה במתנת ש\"מ משמע דנאמנת לדברי הרמב\"ם והרא\"ש שסוברים שאם נתנו במתנת ש\"מ אין צריך לומר קני לך איהו וכל שעבוד' דאית בי' וכמו שנתבאר בטור חשן משפט עכ\"ל ולא נהירא לי דזה לא תלוי בהרמב\"ם והרא\"ש דאע\"ג דסבירא להו דא\"צ לומר קני לך איהו וכל שעבודא היינו כשידוע שנתן אבל מ\"מ אינה נאמנת שנתנה לה במתנת ש\"מ תדע דהא מוכיח כן מעובד' דמלוגא דשטרי דפ' הכותב (דפ\"ה ע\"א) ומהתם יש להוכיח דבמתנת ש\"מ נמי אינה נאמנת דאל\"כ הית' נאמנת הך איתתא דמחיים תפסה במגו זו וכן הביא הב\"י סימן זה סעיף י\"ב תשובת הרשב\"א דלעולם צריך להביא ראיה על הכתיבה ואפי' לרבא כו' וכן אינו נאמן לומר במתנת ש\"מ נתנו לו כדמוכח בפ' הכותב בעובד' דמלוגא דשטרי ע\"כ וכן הביא בשם הנמוקי יוסף שביררו המפרשים שאין תפיסתו ראיה על הכתיבה ולא על האגב וה\"ה אם טען שנתנו לו במתנת ש\"מ צריך להביא ראי' ע\"כ וליכא למימר דהרשב\"א לטעמיה אזיל וכמ\"ש ס\"ס זה ס\"ק קכ\"ב בשמו דש\"מ צ\"ל ג\"כ קני לך איהו וכל שעבודא כו' דמה חילוק יש בזה לענין ראי'. ועוד דהא הר\"ן כתב בפ' הכותב ג\"כ דאינה נאמנת לו' במתנת ש\"מ נתנו לי והרי הב\"י סוף סי' זה כתב שהר\"ן פ' מי שמת כתב כהרמב\"ם דש\"מ א\"צ לומר קני כו' ע\"ש וגם הרמב\"ן בחדושיו פ' גט פשוט דף ק\"ח ע\"ב וכ\"כ הריטב\"א שם בפרק הכותב וכ\"כ הבעה\"ת שער נ\"א ריש ח\"ח וכן הביא הבעה\"ת עוד שם בסוף ח\"ח דברי הר\"ר נתן בהר\"מ שהוכיח דאינו נאמן בשום טענה בין שטען אגב קרקע נתנם לי ובין שטען במתנת ש\"מ נתנם לי והשיג שם על הראב\"ד וכן עיקר וכן נראה דעת הרב בהג\"ה:"]
[" ואפי' היה כו'. נ\"ל שצ\"ל ואם היה וכן הוא בעיר שושן:"]
[" אינו נאמן כו' ואין הלוקח כו'. יש לדקדק אמאי לא ה\"ל הלוה מחוייב שבועה להכחיש השליש שהוא עד ואינו יכול לישבע שהרי אינו יודע ומשלם ולהפוסקים דבדבר דלא ה\"ל לידע לא אמרינן משואיל\"מ י\"ל דהכא נמי לא ה\"ל לידע שמכרו אבל לאינך קשה ונראה דמיירי שהשליש הוא קרוב או פסול וכן בנמוקי יוסף שממנו מקור דין זה איתא כדאמרינן בסנהדרין כו' ובסנהדרין שם בס\"פ זה בורר היה השליש אשה עיין שם ודו\"ק:"]
siftei_kohen.en:
He does not require witnesses for purposes of his acquisition. Many authorities disagree, and the practical halachah follows them, that witnesses are required even to establish the transfer itself, as explained below. Therefore, if the debtor pays the purchaser without the seller's knowledge, he may recover that payment from him, as will be explained below in seif 17. So too writes the Bach. However, if the debtor claims with certainty, "I know that the purchaser had a written transfer document and it was lost," he takes a heset oath and is exempt.
Or he claimed that it was transferred to him together with land. This follows the Rambam and Mechaber above in seif 10, that transfer by agav does not require writing. According to what I wrote there in seif katan 26, however, that agav substitutes only for delivery and written transfer is still required, this argument does not apply. See Responsa Maharit, siman 91.
And if there is proof that he sold it. So writes the Maggid Mishneh. Gidulei Terumah, Shaar 51, end of part 4, folio 312, asks why the Maggid Mishneh requires proof. Even without proof, if the seller himself admits the sale, that should suffice, and migo has no role here, since migo is used to establish one claim because the litigant could have made another, or as a means to avoid an oath. There is no difficulty. A litigant's admission is certainly equivalent to one hundred witnesses. Further, it appears that the Maggid Mishneh deliberately says, "if there is proof," because he means that the seller must pay Reuven the full value of the document. If there is no proof of sale, then even if the seller admits that he sold it and refuses to swear, his refusal does not prove that he was paid only after the sale. Perhaps he had already been paid beforehand. If he were to say explicitly that he had been paid before the sale, in which case he would owe only the money he received for the sale, he would be believed through a migo that he could have denied ever selling it. Therefore, even now, although he refuses to swear, perhaps he refuses because he had been paid before the sale. But where there is proof of sale and he has no migo, he is not believed to say that payment preceded the sale, as I write below in seif katan 35 in the name of the Maggid Mishneh. Consequently, because he refuses to swear, we do not accept the claim that he was paid before the sale, and since the purchaser now suffers loss through his conduct, he must pay the full value of the debt document. This appears correct to me.
He must pay Reuven. This is so even though he did not admit that the debtor paid him, provided that Shimon says, "let him swear to me," as I write in the next seif katan. He must pay the full value of the debt document; returning only the purchase price he received is insufficient. This is implied by the Maggid Mishneh there and is stated explicitly by the Sema, seif katan 31. Although the Maggid Mishneh explicitly writes payment of the full value only where the seller admitted he had been paid, it clearly follows there that the same applies here. Since the seller refuses to swear, he is treated as admitting that he was paid, because the document becomes uncollectible through his conduct. Shiltei Giborim in the name of Ri'az states the same, as I cite below in seif 32, seif katan 109. This is the primary ruling.
And likewise if he admitted, etc. The Mechaber's word "likewise" is somewhat awkward. He should have written: "All the more so if Levi admitted that the debtor paid him." Nevertheless, the rule that if the seller refuses to swear he must pay Reuven applies only when Shimon says, "let him swear to me," as the Rambam and Mechaber state. If Shimon does not demand an oath, even if he says he paid the seller, the seller is not obligated to swear, as below in siman 82, seif 2, and Reuven may collect. Similarly, the later statement that the seller's heirs swear applies only when the debtor says to them, "swear to me," as below in siman 108, seif 5.
If Levi admitted that the debtor paid him, etc. Baal HaTerumos, Shaar 51, part 1, writes regarding this: it is reasonable that this applies only where the debt document does not contain a credibility clause. But if it contains a credibility clause, the purchaser collects from the debtor against his will, and the creditor's admission has no effect, according to those who rule that one is believed to say, "I had a transfer document and it was lost," because we suspect collusion. This does not appear correct to me. Once the creditor himself says that the debt was paid, what difference does a credibility clause make? He himself is declaring that the debt no longer exists, as I wrote above in siman 77, seif katan 4. Further, the reason he is believed to say that it was paid is either his migo that he could have forgiven the debt, or because his statement itself is treated as a present waiver, as I explain in the next seif katan. Both reasons apply even where the debt document contains a credibility clause. This is also implied by the Rambam, Tur, Mechaber, and other poskim, who make no such distinction. This is the primary ruling. A practical difference arises even according to those who disagree and do not believe the purchaser's claim that he had a transfer document and lost it, where the purchaser does possess a written transfer.
Levi admitted that the debtor paid him, etc. This law applies even where Reuven has witnesses to the transfer, because Levi could have forgiven the debt. Through the migo that he could have forgiven it, he is believed when he says that the debt document was paid. Some explain that when he says the debt document is paid, he is effectively forgiving it at that very moment, and there is no greater waiver than this. These are the words of the Maggid Mishneh. I also cite below in seif 16, seif katan 61, in the name of the French authorities and Rabbi Meir son of Rabbi Yehudah that a declaration of payment itself constitutes waiver. Accordingly, not only a claim of payment but any statement that nullifies the document, such as that it was an amanah document, that it was subject to an unfulfilled condition, or the like, is within the seller's power. Rabbeinu Yerucham writes the same at the end of Nesiv 14, cited by the Beit Yosef in this siman, seif 14, and again at the end of this siman, that the seller is believed to say the document was an amanah or was paid. He explains it by the migo that the seller could have forgiven the debt. According to what I have written, no migo is needed. A declaration of amanah, condition, or payment has the same effect as waiver. Admittedly, the Rosh in the second chapter of Kesubos, concerning a person who owes money to others and says a debt owed to him was paid, writes that he is not believed through a migo that he could forgive it because he does not intend to forgive and lose his own debt. Rabbeinu Yerucham, Nesiv 6, part 6, writes similarly. That does not appear consistent with my explanation, because according to them he can in fact forgive even where he owes money to others, and saying that it is paid should itself be the waiver. Nevertheless, the primary ruling appears to me as I have written. It is a strong principle: what difference is there between expressly saying, "I forgive it," and saying, "it has been paid"? According to his own statement the debt document is canceled and extinguished; there is no greater waiver. I reach the same conclusion below in siman 86, seif 5, seif katan 11. According to this, the Gemara at the beginning of Bava Metzia 20a, which says, "this proves that Shmuel's law applies," need not be explained, as some authorities do, that if the woman had intended collusion she could simply have forgiven the ketubah. Rather, the plain explanation is that when she now gives the husband a receipt and says that her ketubah was paid, this itself is the greatest possible waiver. Thus Shmuel's law applies, that one who sells a debt document and later forgives the debt has effected a valid waiver. Shmuel states the greater novelty, that even a gratuitous waiver is effective; all the more so where the seller states that the debt was paid or was merely an amanah and therefore never collectible. Nimukei Yosef there, at the end of Bava Metzia, likewise writes that the case is not based on migo at all. Since she admits that it is paid and the receipt is valid, that itself is her waiver, equivalent to saying, "it is forgiven to you." It appears there that Nimukei Yosef takes this from the Rashba and Ran. Rashi's explanation also appears this way. He writes that since we are not concerned for the possibility that she sold the ketubah and is now producing a receipt, even if that had occurred the husband would properly acquire through the receipt written for her, because Shmuel's law applies. Thus if she sold her ketubah in Iyar and later forgave it to the husband in Tishrei, the waiver is effective and the husband properly defeats the purchaser. Rashi does not mean specifically that she physically wrote a receipt. The same applies if she says the debt was paid, and the receipt merely serves as evidence that the ketubah was paid. Baal HaTerumos, Shaar 51, beginning of part 2, cites a responsum of the Raavad that a seller of a debt document is not believed to say it was paid through a migo that he could have forgiven it, and claims that the Bava Metzia sugya proves this, because the Mishnah speaks of finding a receipt in the marketplace. If mere speech could defeat the purchaser, why discuss a receipt? This does not appear correct to me. In addition, the Ramban, Rosh, Ran at the end of Perek Kol HaNishba'in, the other poskim, the Rambam, Maggid Mishneh, Mechaber here, Baal HaItur, Baal HaTerumos, Tur, and Mechaber below in seif 15 plainly disagree, because they explicitly rule that the seller of a debt document is believed to say that it was paid. Rather, as I explained, the Gemara mentions a receipt because the receipt provides evidence, or because of the continuation of the Mishnah, that where the woman does not admit its validity the receipt is returned to neither party. In truth she is believed by her oral statement alone that the ketubah was paid, either by a migo that she could forgive it or, as I have written, because her very statement that it was paid is the greatest possible waiver. This is contrary to the Raavad's responsum and is the primary ruling.
Levi shall pay Reuven, etc. The Maggid Mishneh writes regarding the Rambam's later phrase, "Levi claims that he did not sell and did not give, etc.," that from the Rambam's inclusion of "did not give" it appears that when Levi says the debt was paid he must compensate Reuven like one who forgives an assigned debt, as explained below in seif 32, who must pay the full amount of the document. Thus, even if he sold it for one hundred while it was worth one thousand, the person who forgave it pays one thousand. So too here, when Levi says it was paid, he pays the full value of the debt document. We do not believe him to say that it had already been paid before the sale. It appears to me that this assumes there are witnesses that he sold it. Otherwise, he would be believed that payment preceded the sale through a migo that he could deny the sale. Even though denying a sale would be a brazen claim while his present claim is not, a migo of that type is accepted, as I write below in siman 81, seif 23, seif katan 58, and siman 93, seif 2, and as I prove below at the end of siman 82 in the laws of migo, letter 6. If payment preceded the sale, he would owe only the purchase price he received because the sale was a transaction in something that did not exist. Although we believe him with respect to the debtor because he could forgive the debt, he is certainly liable in damages to the purchaser just as he would be if he actually forgave it. Otherwise, even if Levi admitted that he gave the document as a gift, he would pay nothing if we believed him that payment occurred before the gift, because he would have given something with no value. One could answer that when the Rambam says, "and did not give," he means that he gave it without responsibility, or alternatively that he did not give it and only afterward received payment. Nevertheless, the primary law appears as the Maggid Mishneh explained. His words are correct, the Rambam likewise appears to hold this way, and the attempted alternative is strained. I also cite below in seif 32, seif katan 109, Shiltei Giborim in the name of Ri'az to the same effect. The Mechaber likewise appears to rule this way, and it is primary. It further appears that even if the debtor did not pay the seller the full face value, but the seller claims he accepted only an amount equal to what he had received for the sale and thereby agreed that the debt should be treated as paid, he must nevertheless pay the purchaser the full value of the document, because the document was lost through his conduct. There is no difficulty from Baal HaTerumos, Tur, and Mechaber below in seif 34, who rule that if the debtor produces a receipt showing that this debt document was paid, the transaction is a mistaken sale and the purchase money is returned, implying that the seller need return only what he received. There, the debtor produces an independent receipt, so even without the seller's admission it is established that he sold a paid document. The sale was therefore void from inception and the purchase price is returned. Here, by contrast, there is no proof that the debt was paid other than Levi's admission. Had Levi wished to swear, Reuven could have collected from Shimon against Shimon's will. It is therefore Levi's admission, or his refusal to swear, which is equivalent to an admission, that prevents Reuven from collecting. Levi is effectively forgiving the debt now and causing the purchaser's loss now. He must therefore pay the full value of the debt document. Shiltei Giborim in the name of Ri'az, cited below in seif 32, seif katan 109, appears to make this very distinction, and it is primary. This also answers, in my humble opinion, the Rosh's question at the end of Perek Shnayim Ochazin on the Gemara's statement, "this proves that Shmuel's law applies": if the woman forgives the ketubah she will have to pay the purchaser the full value of the ketubah. The Rosh cites those who infer from this that one who forgives an assigned debt need repay only the amount the purchaser paid. In my humble opinion, the one who forgives must pay the full value of the debt document, as I write below in seif 32, seif katan 109. The Gemara's statement is nevertheless correct, because in its present case too she must compensate the purchaser for the full value. The receipt is returned only because of her admission. Without her admission, the receipt would not be returned. Thus the ketubah is lost through her conduct, and she is equivalent to one who presently forgives the ketubah. This appears clear to me. Nimukei Yosef in the first chapter of Bava Metzia also plainly implies this.
And if they do not wish to swear, they pay the purchaser. This implies that they pay him the full value of the document, and the same is implied by the Maggid Mishneh. Further, according to the Sema's explanation in seif katan 31, the Mechaber's earlier phrase, "he must pay Reuven," means the full value of the debt document. Presumably, therefore, the Mechaber's phrase here, "they pay the purchaser," likewise means the full value. All liabilities their father bore are presumptively inherited by them. The two clauses also presumptively concern the same type of liability; otherwise, the Mechaber should have distinguished them expressly. There is no reason to distinguish between the father and the heirs. It is not reasonable to say that because the father was the seller he owes more. He owes more than the purchase money he received, and even if he gave the document as a gift he must pay. Rather, the basis of liability is that by refusing to swear he causes the purchaser a loss and is therefore liable under the law of garmi for the damage he causes. That reasoning applies equally to the heirs. One might say that the heirs can claim, "we do not intend to harm the purchaser; we know the debt was paid and do not wish to swear falsely." But the seller or donor could make the identical claim. Necessarily, because they cannot substantiate their assertion they are liable under the law of garmi, as I write below in seif 32, seif katan 105, in the name of Shiltei Giborim citing Ri'az. The same therefore applies to heirs. This is clear. It also contradicts the Sema's words below in seif 15, seif katan 41, as I explain there in seif katan 53.
Levi claimed that he did not sell, etc. Meaning, Levi makes this claim against Reuven, and Levi then swears. The Beit Yosef and Kesef Mishneh, however, explain that Levi makes this claim against Shimon and that Shimon swears. This is not satisfactory. The Sema, seif katan 33, writes that they did not explain the Rambam according to its plain meaning because they hold that if Levi admits the debt was paid but says to Reuven, "I never sold it to you," Levi would not even need to swear, since the burden of proof is upon the claimant. This does not appear correct. Why should Levi not swear? According to Reuven's certain claim, Levi owes him money. The plain meaning of the Rambam is therefore as I have explained. The Maggid Mishneh explicitly explains it this way, and the Beit Yosef cites him. The Rama also writes in responsum 95, question 2, that Levi swears, and says that the Beit Yosef agrees, merely adding on his own that Shimon also takes a heset oath. The Bach likewise writes that even the Beit Yosef agrees to Levi's oath as a matter of law, and the Ir Shushan says the same. See there.
That even with respect to its acquisition, etc. See the Ir Shushan, who writes that the physical paper of the document must be returned to him. The same is stated by Baal HaTerumos, Shaar 51, part 8, in the name of Rabbi Nasan son of Rabbi Meir, and by the Ran in Perek HaKosev concerning the incident of the bundle of documents, as I wrote above in siman 64, seif katan 4.
He is not believed. It follows that the same applies if he claims, "it was given to me as a deathly ill person's gift," and he is not believed, contrary to what the Beit Yosef writes in Even HaEzer, siman 86. He cites Responsa Ramban, siman 30, concerning debt documents claimed by the guardians. If the woman claims that her husband gave them to her, the guardians prevail, because a debt document is acquired only through writing and delivery. This remains so even where there are no witnesses and no present sight of the documents, because migo does not apply to documents in this context, as the Rif writes in Perek HaKosev concerning the bundle of documents. The Beit Yosef then adds that if she says they were given to her as a gift of a shechiv mera, she would apparently be believed according to the Rambam and Rosh, who hold that in a shechiv mera gift the giver need not say, "Acquire it and all the lien contained in it," as explained in Tur Choshen Mishpat. This does not appear correct to me. The issue does not depend on that dispute. Even according to the Rambam and Rosh, who hold that the special transfer formula is unnecessary in a shechiv mera gift, that applies where the gift itself is known. It does not establish that the possessor is believed to say that such a gift occurred. Proof is the incident of the bundle of documents in Perek HaKosev, Kesubos 85a, from which this very point is derived. That case also proves that she is not believed even to say that they were given to her as a shechiv mera gift, for otherwise the woman who seized them during the deceased's lifetime would have been believed through that migo. The Beit Yosef in this siman, seif 12, likewise cites a responsum of the Rashba that one always needs proof of the written transfer, even according to Rava, and that one is likewise not believed to say that the documents were given as a shechiv mera gift, as proved by the incident of the bundle of documents in Perek HaKosev. He also cites Nimukei Yosef that the commentators clarified that possession is no proof either of written transfer or of acquisition through agav, and the same applies to a claim that the documents were given as a shechiv mera gift, which requires proof. One cannot answer that the Rashba follows his own view, cited by me at the end of this siman, seif katan 122, that even a shechiv mera must say, "Acquire it and all its liens," because that has no bearing on the evidentiary question. Further, the Ran in Perek HaKosev also writes that she is not believed to say, "he gave it to me as a shechiv mera gift," while the Beit Yosef himself writes at the end of this siman that in Perek Mi SheMes the Ran follows the Rambam that a shechiv mera need not use the special transfer formula. The Ramban in his novellae to Perek Get Pashut, folio 108b, and the Ritva in Perek HaKosev likewise say so. Baal HaTerumos, Shaar 51, beginning of part 8, writes the same, and at the end of that part cites Rabbi Nasan in the name of Rabbi Meir, who proves that one is not believed on any such claim, whether he says, "he gave them to me together with land," or, "he gave them to me as a shechiv mera gift." He there challenges the Raavad. This is the primary ruling, and the Rama in the gloss also appears to follow it.
And even if it was, etc. It appears to me that the text should read, "And if it was," as in the Ir Shushan.
He is not believed, etc., and the purchaser does not, etc. One can ask why the debtor should not be obligated to take an oath contradicting the third party, who is a single witness, and then be required to pay because he cannot swear, since he does not know. According to those poskim who hold that we do not say, "one who is obligated to swear and cannot swear must pay," where the matter was not something he should have known, one can answer that here too the debtor had no reason to know that the document had been sold. But according to the other authorities the question remains. It appears that the case concerns a third party who is a relative or otherwise disqualified as a witness. Nimukei Yosef, which is the source of this ruling, cites the case as discussed in Sanhedrin, and there, at the end of Perek Zeh Borer, the third party was a woman. See there carefully.

turei_zahav.he: (בטור עא"ע דאפילו למאן דבעי כתיב' א"צ וכו') ע' בר"ן פ' הכותב שהביאו מהא דדייקינן בפ' ג"פ דב' יב"ש הדרין בעיר א' מוציאין ש"ח על אחרים ומפרשים דס"ל כרבא כו' הלכך לדידן דק"ל דאין אותיות לקנות במסירה ע"כ טעמא דמוציאין משום דיכול לטעון כתב קנין הי' לי ואבד וא"צ להביא ראיה עכ"ל מבואר דס"ל דגם נגד הלוה א"צ ראיה ולכך מוציאין על אחרים ודלא כרמב"ם ומ"ש ב"י דדעת הרא"ש כהר"י מגא"ש ליתא ודו"ק:
turei_zahav.en: (In the Tur: Even according to the authority who requires writing, it is unnecessary, etc.) See the Ran in HaKotev, who derives from the rule that two men named Yosef ben Shimon in one city may produce debt instruments against others. Since documentary rights are not acquired by delivery alone, the present holder must be believed to say that he once had a written transfer and lost it, without bringing proof. This shows that even against the debtor no additional proof is required, contrary to the Rambam. The Beit Yosef’s attribution of the Rosh to Rabbi Yosef Migash is therefore incorrect.

urim_vetumim_tumim.he: לא קנאם וכו' והש"ך הביא תשובת ריטב"א דס"ל בכלל נכסי אף שעבוד בכלל נכסיו וכשאמר נכסי אף שעבוד ניתן וכאומר קני לך איהו וכל שעבודא: ואולי הריטב"א לשיטתו דס"ל מכירת שטרות דאורייתא והיינו דיש להמלוה יד בשעבודו של לוה ונכסיו עד שיכול למוכרן ולכך שפיר י"ל דשעבוד בכלל נכסיו דהרי הוא בכלל שחל עליו מכירה אבל לפי דקי"ל מכירת שטרות ליתא ד"ת דאין כאן שום ממש שיחול עליו הקנין דאין למלוה ברשותו דבר וב"ח מכאן ולהבא גובה אף בכלל נכסי לא שייכי ולא חל הלשון נכסי כלל אשעבוד. ובאמת זה תלי' במחלוק' דלקמן סי' רנ"ג בש"מ שאמר שטרי לפלוני אי צ"ל קני לך איהו וכל שעבודא או אין צריך דאי צריך לכאורה הדבר מוכרח כמ"ש הריטב"א דהא אמרינן ש"מ שאמר נכסי לפלוני שטרי בכלל מדתניא וכו' וקשה בממ"נ אי אמר בפי' הן וכל שעבוד' מה צריך לראי' הא אמר להדיא הן וכל שעבוד' וחזינא דנתכוון לשטרות והכי דייק הרא"ש בתשובה כלל ע"ה ד"ב דלא היה שם מסירה בשטר ע"ש ואי לא אמר מה יהני דשטר בכלל נכסי הא צ"ל הן וכל שעבודן ועכצ"ל כריטב"א דנכסי הוי כמו כל שעבודן ומזה יליף הריטב"א דינו עיי' בנ"י. כי מ"ש בקדושין מהך כאותו ששנינו נכסי' שיש להם אחריות וכו' אין כאן ראי' דבאמת כתב רשב"א בחדושיו דצ"ל קני לך איהו וכו' והגמ' מקצר דכמו דצ"ל אגב וקני ולא נזכר בגמ'. אבל לפי דעת המחבר ורוב פוסקים כמש"ל בסי' רנ"ג דא"צ לומר כלל בש"מ איהו וכל שעבוד דאי' בי'. א"כ אין כאן ראי' כלל מהך דשטרות בכלל נכסי א"כ מי מכריח אותנו לדוחק הלזה דשעבוד בכלל נכסי' ובפרט אי מכירות אותיות דרבנן וכמ"ש וכ"כ דאין לנו ראי' ברורה מהכ"ת לומר כן. אלא דקשי' ליה על רשב"א דהוא סובר כהך רבוות' דש"מ שאמר שטרי לפלוני צ"ל קני איהו וכל שעבודא דאי' בי': וא"כ ראי' הנ"ל מוכרח ומ"מ פסק דאין שעבוד' בכלל נכסים וקו' הנ"ל במקומו וצ"ל דס"ל לרשב"א באמת הא דאצטריך הגמ' להביא ראי' דשטרו' בכלל נכסי' נ"מ בשטרות דא"צ לומר קני לך איהו דהיינו שכתב בו לכל המוציאו דא"צ לומר כלל וכל שעבוד' דשעבוד' ממילא חל דהרי נשתעבד לכל המוציאו וסגי בקנין חליפין כמש"ל וא"כ אצ"ל כלל להלוקח ומקבל כל שעבוד' דאי' בי' ובזה קמ"ל הגמר' באומר נכסי סתם דשטרי בכלל נכסי אינן. משא"כ בשארי שטרות פשיטא דלא נ"מ כלל דבממ"נ אי אמר הן וכל שעבודן הא אמר ואי לאו מ"מ לא מהני ודוק וזה ראי' ג"כ לדידן הנ"ל דבכה"ג שטרות אפי' אמירה א"צ שוב ראיתי בנ"י פ' הספינה משמע דס"ל לרשב"א לחלק בש"מ גופי' באומר שטרי צריך לומר איהו וכל שעבודא אבל באומר נכסי בכולל הקילו עליו דאצ"ל והדבר דחוק בעצמותו וגם מנ"ל להגמ' הא דהא הגמ' הביא ראי' מהך כאותו ששנינו נכסי' שיש להם וכו' ושם הא פירש הרשב"א להדיא כמש"ל דצ"ל קני וכו' ולכן יותר ברור כמש"ל וצ"ע כי לשונו בתשובה לא משמע כן דכתב דא"א להעמידו בבריא ואם כמ"ש אף בבריא יכול להעמידו בהקנה לו אגב קרקע וכדומה ולכן נוטי' הדברים דס"ל לרשב"א דלשון נכסי אי גם שעבודא בכלל או לא הדבר סתום ובבריא אמר אי איתא דנתכוון לשעבודא ה"ל לפרש משא"כ בש"מ דלא שייך כן דלקצר קעביד ולכך אף שעבוד בכלל וזה דוחק. וגם מה ראי' יש כמש"ל דשם לא מיירי אלא דגוף שטר בכלל נכסי' ולא שעבוד דהא בבריא באמת אין שעבוד בכלל וצ"ע:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en: He did not acquire them, and so forth. Shach cites a responsum of Ritva holding that when one says, "I give you my property," the word "property" includes his debt rights as well. It is therefore as though he had said, "Acquire the note and all its liens." Perhaps Ritva follows his own view that sale of debt documents is of Torah force. On that understanding, the lender has a genuine proprietary interest in the borrower's lien and assets that can be treated as part of "my property." But according to our halachah that sale of ordinary debt documents is not of Torah force, there is no tangible asset in the lender's possession upon which an ordinary proprietary transfer can operate. A creditor collects only prospectively. The debt lien is therefore not naturally included in the word "my property." This issue appears to depend on the dispute below in siman 253 concerning a deathbed person who says, "My documents to so-and-so." Must he also say, "Acquire them and all the liens contained in them"? If one requires the additional language, Ritva's position seems almost compelled by the Gemara's statement that when a deathbed person says, "My property to so-and-so," his debt documents are included. If "property" did not include the debt lien, what would the Gemara gain by saying the papers themselves are included? The beneficiary still would not acquire the debts. One could say that the deathbed person explicitly said "the documents and all their liens," but then there would be no need for the Gemara's proof that documents are included in "property"; his express words already identify them. Thus, under the view requiring the special phrase when documents are given specifically, the broader word "my property" must itself include the liens. This is likely Ritva's proof. Rashba, however, complicates matters. He holds that when a deathbed person specifically gives his documents, he must say "them and all their liens," yet elsewhere he appears to hold that a general gift of "my property" does not automatically include the debt liens. One possible answer is that the Gemara's proof that documents are included in "property" is needed only for special bearer notes that require no separate phrase "and all their liens." If the note says "to whoever produces it," the borrower's lien already follows the paper. Then the only question is whether the physical note is included in the word "property." The Gemara teaches that it is. This also supports what I wrote above that bearer notes require no additional transfer formula. Nimukei Yosef in Perek HaSefinah suggests another distinction within deathbed gifts themselves: if the dying person says specifically, "my documents," he must add the lien language, but if he gives "all my property," Chazal treated the broader gift more leniently. That is difficult and lacks a clear source. Perhaps Rashba instead regards the meaning of "property" as context dependent. In an ordinary healthy person's transaction, where precise drafting is expected, if he intended debt liens he should have said so. A deathbed declaration is normally brief and informal, and we therefore interpret "my property" broadly enough to include the liens. This too is somewhat strained. At any rate, outside the special deathbed context there is no clear proof that the general word "property" transfers ordinary debt liens. Especially under the accepted view that sale of documents is rabbinic, we should not assume such an unusual proprietary meaning without express language. Therefore Ritva's broad ruling should not be extended beyond the contexts in which the authorities clearly adopted it.

urim_vetumim_urim.he: שכתוב בו וכו'. הרב הש"ך האריך לחלוק ועיין תומים דבררתי לא זו בשטר שכתב לכל המוציאו הוא הדין בכתב לך ולכל דאתא מחמתך אין צריך כתיבה ומסירה. ומ"מ הן כתב דאתא מחמתך או כתב לכל מי שמוציאו כיון שנזכר מתחילה שם המלוה המלוה ראשון יכול למחול לדעת החולקים אראב"ד לקמן בסעיף כ"ו דאין תליא זה בזה כמ"ש הש"ך ועיין תומים ואם מחל אם צריך המוחל לשלם עיין מש"ל:
urim_vetumim_urim.en: In which it is written, etc. Shach argues at length. See Tumim. I establish that not only an instrument saying “to whoever produces it,” but also one saying “to you and anyone who comes by your authority,” does not require separate written assignment and delivery. Nevertheless, in either formulation, if the original lender's name is mentioned first, the original lender may still be able to waive the debt according to the authorities who disagree with Raavad below in seif 26. The question whether assignment form and power of waiver are linked is separate, as Shach himself notes. See Tumim. If the lender waives the debt, whether he must compensate the assignee is discussed above.

mechaber.he: מכנסת לבעלה שטר אינו צריך כתיבה ומסירה ואם הוא מלוה על פה אינו צריך מעמד שלשתן ואפי' אם היו נכסי מלוג:
mechaber.en: Entering her husband, who does not need writing and delivery, and if he is affiliated with it, he does not need the status of their drinking and character if they were property:

baer_hetev.he: מכנסת. הטעם דידו כידה ואין קנין לאשה בלא בעלה ועי' בא"ע סימן צ"א. סמ"ע:
baer_hetev.en: Entering. The taste of Dedda, and there is no property for a woman without her husband and her husband. A:

beer_hagolah.he: י) כן השיב הרמב"ן שקנה בתקנת חכמים מס"ב
beer_hagolah.en: So the Ramban answered, that he acquires through a rabbinic enactment.

beur_hagra.he:
מכנסת. דאין קנין לאשה בלא בעלה שלכן אינו יכול למחול כמש"ל בסכ"ח והטעם דגוף הלוה משועבד לו ג"כ ומה"ט א"צ כו"מ:
(ליקוט) מכנסת כו'. שגוף הלואה קנוי לו ודמי כמו במתנת ש"מ כמ"ש קנ"א א' והא לא משך וכמו שמדמי לענין מחילה כמש"ל סכ"ז וסכ"ח (ע"כ):
ואם הוא. ואפי'. ע' בסכ"ח:
beur_hagra.en:
She brings into the marriage. A married woman has no independent power of acquisition against her husband, which is why he cannot forgive the debt, as explained below in seif 28. The reason is that the underlying loan obligation itself becomes subject to him. For this reason no writing and delivery are required.
(Collected note) She brings into the marriage... The underlying loan itself is acquired by him. It is comparable to a gift of a shechiv mera, as in Bava Batra 151a, "but he did not pull it," and as the Gemara compares them regarding forgiveness, as explained below in seifim 27 and 28. (End of note.)
And if it is. Even... See seif 28.

chelkat_mechokek.he: ויקבל עליו אחריות אם יאבדו. משמע דאף דהאשה רוצה לקבל המטלטלין על האחריות שלה לא שרי כי היכא דבכל אשה קי"ל אם התפיסה צררי ונאבדו נאבדו לו כדאיתא ר"פ אעפ"י ומיהו יש לחלק בין התפסה זו שהיא רק לשעה להתפס' צררי דעלמא דהתם יש לחוש שמא יאמר טלי כתובתך וצאי אם יהיו על אחריות שלה אבל בהתפס' זו שהיא רק לשעה לא חיישינן אפילו באחריות שלה ע"כ השמיטו הפוסקים דבר זה ולא נמצא רק בסמ"ג לבד וגם הסמ"ג אפשר דמיירי אם היא אינה רוצה לקבל אחריו' אביד' וזול אבל אם היא מרוצ' לכך אין בזה קפידא בהתפסה זו שהיא רק לשעה אחר שכתבתי זה ראיתי בדברי התוספות בכתובות בדף נ"ו ע"ב בד"ה אין עושין כתובות אשה מטלטלין מפני תיקון העולם פרש"י שמא יפחתו דמיהן או יאבדו והא דאמרינן בפ"ק א"ר אמי שרי למבעל בתולה בשבת אמרו ליה רבנן והא לא כתיבא כתובת' אמר להו אתפסוה מטלטלין מיירי שקבל עליו אחריות אם יאבדו או יזולו וע"ש בדבור שאח"ז:
chelkat_mechokek.en: And he accepts responsibility if they are lost. This implies that even if the woman agrees to accept the movable property at her own risk, it is not permitted. Ordinarily, if a husband places valuables in her possession for her ketubah and they are lost, the loss is his, as stated at the beginning of chapter Af Al Pi. One can distinguish, however, between this temporary security and an ordinary long-term placement of assets. In the ordinary case, if the assets were at her risk, there would be concern that the husband might say, "Take your ketubah and leave," because the assets would effectively already be hers. But with this temporary arrangement, perhaps that concern does not apply even if she accepts the risk. This may be why most authorities omit this requirement and it appears only in Semag. Semag himself may mean only that if she refuses to accept the risk of loss or depreciation, the husband must accept it, but if she willingly assumes it there is no objection in a temporary arrangement. After writing this I saw Tosafot, Ketubot 56b, who explain Rashi's statement that movable property is not designated for a ketubah because its value may depreciate or it may be lost. Tosafot reconcile the first chapter, where Rav Ami permitted first relations on Shabbat after they placed movable property in the bride's possession, by explaining that the husband accepted responsibility if it was lost or depreciated. See also the following Tosafot passage.

haggahot_imrei_barukh.he: (ש"ך ס"ק פא) בס' הזכו' דא"י למחול. נ"ב יעוין מ"ש הרמב"ן בחידושיו במס' יבמות על דף מ"ה ע"ב בד"ה וקדם וטבל כו':
haggahot_imrei_barukh.en: (Shach, seif katan 81) In Sefer HaZechut, that he cannot waive it. Note: See what Ramban writes in his novellae to Yevamot 45b, s.v. 'and he preceded and immersed,' etc.

meirat_einayim.he: מכנסת לבעלה שט"ח כו' הטעם דידה כידו ואין קנין לאשה בלא בעלה ועד"מ ובהגהותיו מ"ש בזה ועיין בא"ע סי' צ"א:
meirat_einayim.en: A woman brings a debt instrument into the marriage to her husband, etc. The reason is that her legal hand is like his, and a wife cannot acquire independently of her husband. See Darkei Moshe and its glosses for what is written on this, and see Even HaEzer siman 91.

netivot_hamishpat_beurim.he: מכנסת לבעלה שטר חוב החלקת מחוקק והבית שמואל באה"ע סי' נ"א ס"ק ב' כתבו דאם הלוה טוען פרעתי צריכה לישבע ואם אינה רוצה לישבע לא יפרע הלוה ע"ש. ונראה דס"ל כשיטת המחבר בח"מ סי' מ"ז דאפי' בחב לאחרים דאינו יכול למחול בעינן דוקא כתוב בו נאמנות ובאם לא אינו גובה א"כ ה"ה במכנסת לבעלה שט"ח. אבל דעת הש"ך שם ס"ק ד' דבחב לאחרים כיון שאינו יכול למחול אפי' אין כתוב בו נאמנות וא"י לישבע אפ"ה גובה א"כ ה"ה במכנסת שט"ח לבעלה כיון דא"י לישבע אפי' אינו רוצה לישבע ואין כתוב בו נאמנות גובה וכן מוכח ברא"ש ור"ן בפ' כל הנשבעין שכתבו הטעם שבועת המוכר משום דנאמן לומר פרוע במיגו דמחיל משמע במקום דא"י למחול דא"נ לומר פרוע דלית ליה מיגו אין מקום לשבועה זו:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: A woman who brings a debt instrument into the marriage. Chelkat Mechokek and Beit Shmuel in Even HaEzer siman 51, seif katan 2, write that if the debtor says he paid, the woman must swear, and if she refuses to swear the debtor does not pay. They appear to follow the Mechaber's position in Choshen Mishpat siman 47 that even where a creditor's admission would injure others and he cannot forgive the debt, collection still requires an express clause of trustworthiness. Without such a clause he cannot collect. The same would therefore apply where a woman brings a debt instrument into marriage. The Shach there, seif katan 4, however, holds that where an admission would injure others and the creditor cannot forgive the debt, collection is permitted even without a trustworthiness clause and even where the creditor cannot swear. The same should apply to a woman who brings a debt instrument into marriage. Since she cannot forgive the debt, collection is allowed even if she cannot or will not swear and the document contains no trustworthiness clause. This is also indicated by Rosh and Ran in the chapter Kol HaNishba'in. They explain the seller's oath by saying that the seller is believed to say the debt was paid through a migo that he could forgive it. This implies that where he cannot forgive the debt, so that there is no such migo and he is not believed to say it was paid, there is no basis for requiring that oath.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: מכנסת לבעלה. דידו כידה ומה"ט א"י למחול) (וא"נ לומר פרוע וכן אפילו אינה רוצה לישבע גובה מבעל וע"ב:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en: Entering her husband. Dodda and the “T” to the dance (and he does not want to say wild and does not even want to swear height from the husband and father:

pitchei_teshuva.he: ראובן שיש לו שטר כו'. עמ"ש לעיל סי' ל"ז סעיף י"א כשם ת' נו"ב:
pitchei_teshuva.en: Reuven who has a debt instrument, etc. See what I wrote above, siman 37, seif 11, in the name of Responsa Noda BiYehuda.

rabbi_akiva_eiger.he: [שו"ע] אין לוי חשוב נוגע. נ"ב ודוקא כשהוחזק השטר בב"ד קודם שמכרו ללוי וכדלעיל סי' מ"ו ס' ל"ד מל"מ פ"ז מה' מכירה:
rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: There is no important thing about it. N.A. and Dukke, when the chairman of the High Court first sold to Loy and jacket C. M. S. L. M. C. M. M. M. C. M. M. M. M. M. M. M. M. M. urim_vetumim_tumim.he: שצריך מסירת השטר קודם וכתב הסמ"ע דה"ה בבת א' ג"כ מועיל ולא אתא אלא לאפוקי דאין להקדים הכתיבה למסירה והש"ך בס"ק י"ד פקפק דאין לסמ"ע ראי' בזה. ואולם בסעיף שלפני זה בנותן כל נכסיו א"ק וכתב בשטר ההוא איהו וכל שעבוד' מועיל אף דהמסירה וכתיבה באי' כאחד כי כשזיכה בקרקע וה"ל מסירה אז חל כתיבה ג"כ וזהו ראי' ברורה לדברי הסמ"ע אך מ"מ פקפק הש"ך דא"א לצמצם ולכך טוב לעשות מסירה מקדם ועל זה אינו ראי' מהך דלעיל דשם ודאי באים כאחד:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en: The document must first be delivered. Sema writes that simultaneous writing and delivery also works. The rule excludes only a case where the writing precedes the delivery. Shach, seif katan 14, questions whether Sema has proof. But the preceding seif provides a clear proof. Where one gives all of his property through a land-based acquisition and the transfer document itself contains the phrase "the note and all its liens," the acquisition is effective even though the writing and delivery occur simultaneously. At the moment the transferee acquires the land, the note is also delivered through the same acquisition, and the written transfer language becomes effective at that very moment. Thus simultaneous writing and delivery must suffice. Shach's further practical recommendation, that because exact simultaneity may be difficult to establish one should perform the delivery first, can still be sensible. The preceding case proves only that legal simultaneity is sufficient where the structure of the transaction makes both elements arise together with certainty. But as a matter of principle, Sema is correct.

chelkat_mechokek.he: ודוקא שכתבה לו התקבלתי. הוסיף הרב מהרמ"א תיבת ודוקא ע"פ המרדכי שכ' בפ' החובל על הא דאמרי' כל לגבי בעל ודאי מחלה ודוקא ע"י שכותבה התקבלתי אבל במחילה בעלמא לא הוי מחילה כשכבר נשואה ואף על גב דבשט"ח פסק המרדכי בסנהדרין דמהני מחילה ואפילו תפס שטרא ומביא ראיה ברורה ומהא דאמרי' המוכר ש"ח לחבירו וחזר ומוחלו מחיל אפשר לחלק דבכתובה באשה היושבת תחת בעלה כל זמן שאינה כותבת לו התקבלתי יכולה לומר משחקת הייתי בך ודברי הבאי אמרתי ולאחר מות בעלה משמע מדברי המרדכי שם דאף בכתובה מהני מחילה גרידא דמייתי ראיה התם מאשה ששהתה כ"ה שנה ולא תבעה כתובתה ע"ש ומ"מ צריך לדקדק מנ"ל למרדכי האי דינא לחלק בכתובה באשה היושבת תחת בעלה דלא מועיל מחילה עד דכותב לו התקבלתי ובגמרא בכתובות דף נ"ו ע"א ר' יהודה אומר אם רוצה כותב לבתולה שטר של מאתים והיא כותבת קבלתי ממך מנה וכו' וקאמר בגמרא טעמא דכתבה ליה אבל על פה דהוי תנאה בעלמא לא הוי תנאה דמתנה על מה שכתוב בתורה הוא ואח"ז בדף הנ"ל ע"ב מייתי פלוגתא דר' יוסי דס"ל רשאי ופרש"י ואפילו ע"פ נמי תנאו קיים ועיין בדף נ"ז ע"א אי פלוגתא דר' יהודה ור' יוסי בתחלה או בסוף והרמב"ם פי"ו מה"א פסק המוחלת כתובתה אינה צריכה קנין ולא עדים כשאר המוחלין שאינן צריכין קנין ולא עדים אלא בדברים בלבד ועיין לקמן סי' ק"ה ובב"ח רצה ליישב ואין דבריו ברורים:
chelkat_mechokek.en: Specifically if she wrote to him, "I have received it." The Rama added the word "specifically" based on Mordechai, chapter HaChovel, who says that the rule "with respect to her husband she certainly waived" applies specifically where she writes, "I have received it." A mere oral waiver is not effective while she remains married. Although regarding an ordinary debt document Mordechai in Sanhedrin rules that an oral waiver is effective even if the creditor retains the document, and brings a clear proof from the rule that one who sells a debt document may later waive it, one can distinguish a ketubah held by a woman living with her husband. So long as she has not written "I have received it," she may say, "I was merely joking with you and spoke idle words." After the husband's death, Mordechai implies that even a simple waiver of a ketubah is effective, for he brings proof from a woman who remained silent for twenty-five years without claiming her ketubah. Still, Mordechai's source for distinguishing a married woman's ketubah from other debts requires precision. Ketubot 56a states Rabbi Yehudah's view that if he wishes he may write a virgin a document for two hundred and she writes, "I have received one hundred from you." The Gemara infers that writing is required, whereas an oral condition is ineffective because it contradicts a Torah entitlement. But immediately afterward the Gemara cites Rabbi Yose, who holds that he may stipulate, and Rashi explains that even orally the condition is valid. Ketubot 57a discusses whether their dispute concerns the beginning or the end of the arrangement. Rambam, Hilchot Ishut chapter 16, rules that one who waives her ketubah needs neither a kinyan nor witnesses, just like other waivers, and mere words suffice. See below, siman 105. The Bach attempts a reconciliation, but his words are not clear.
